He gives snow like wool, and scatters frost like ashes. (Psalm 147:16)
Brothers and sisters, friends, peace to you! Today we step into the Beauty Hall of "Creation Speaks," and our first stop is a little guest who falls from the sky: the snowflake.

Friends who live in the tropics or subtropics might say, "Pastor, I've never touched snow in my life." That's all right. You've surely seen it in photos, on cards, on Christmas decorations. That six-pointed, star-like shape, everyone recognizes it.

But let me ask you a question: have you ever really looked closely at a snowflake? Not a pile of snow, but one single flake. Under a magnifying glass, a snowflake looks like a finely carved six-pointed star: six arms, each sprouting delicate branches and patterns. And then? It lasts just a few seconds before melting in your palm.

Think about it. A work of art that took so much effort, and it's on display for only a few seconds. If people were running this exhibition, the boss would say, "This isn't worth it at all!" But God doesn't seem to care whether it's "worth it." Today, from this little "not worth it" snowflake, we're going to see God's beautiful, good heart.
A farmer who fell in love with snowflakes

More than a hundred years ago, in Vermont, there was a farmer named Wilson Bentley. From the time he was a boy, he was fascinated by snowflakes. On snowy days, when everyone else hid indoors by the fire, he ran outside looking for ways to capture them.

On January 15, 1885, he became the first to photograph a snowflake using a microscope and a camera. From then on, over his lifetime, he took more than 5,000 snowflake photographs. Late in life, he and the meteorologist W. J. Humphreys co-authored a book called Snow Crystals.

Think about that, friends: more than five thousand! If it were us, we'd probably get to picture number fifty and say, "Okay, snowflakes all look pretty much the same." But the more Bentley photographed, the more amazed he became, because he found that every one was different.
In the book of Job, God asks Job a very interesting question:
Out of whose womb came the ice? The gray frost of the sky, who has given birth to it? (Job 38:29)
This is an invitation: an invitation to stop and think. This ice, this frost, these snowflakes, where do they really come from? Today we'll look at three main points.
1. The secret of the hexagon: great order in a tiny lattice
First question: why do snowflakes almost always have six points? Not five, not eight?

The answer is hidden somewhere the naked eye can't see: in water molecules. When water freezes, its molecules join hands through a force called "hydrogen bonding" and line up in a hexagonal lattice. A snowflake's sixfold symmetry is that tiny lattice, scaled all the way up until our eyes can see it.

Here's an analogy. If the bricks you build a house with are themselves hexagonal, then however you stack them, the house will naturally take on a hexagonal look. The snowflake's "blueprint" was already written into its smallest bricks.
Temperature and humidity are the sculptors
So why are some snowflakes thin plates, some columns, and some beautiful stars? That brings us to two sculptors: temperature and humidity.

At about minus 2 degrees Celsius, snow crystals grow as thin plates; at about minus 5 degrees, as columns and fine needles; at about minus 15 degrees, they grow into the most beautiful branching stars. And the more water vapor in the air, the faster the arms grow and the more they branch.

In 1936 the Japanese physicist Ukichiro Nakaya became the first to make artificial snow crystals in the laboratory, and he organized the relationship between temperature, water vapor, and crystal shape into a chart, later called the "Nakaya diagram." He left us a beautiful saying: "Snow crystals are letters sent from heaven."

Brothers and sisters, here is something well worth pondering: snowflakes are not beautiful because they bumped into beauty by random luck, but because the water molecules at the very bottom already have order in them. Beauty is built on order, and order is built on deeper laws.

This leads us to a reasonable inference: a world filled with order even in its tiniest parts points to a wise Creator. The psalm says, "He gives snow like wool, and scatters frost like ashes." To the psalmist, snowfall is not a random weather event but the work of God's own hand.
2. No two alike: every flake keeps its own diary
Our second point is the saying we so often hear: "No two snowflakes in the world are alike." Is that actually true?
Let's start with an analogy. A snowflake is like a diary. As it falls from the cloud, it passes through different temperatures and humidities, and each stage of the journey writes a line on its arms.

You might ask: then why do the six arms of the same snowflake look almost identical? Because those six arms go through the same journey "at the same time," so they write almost the same words. But no two snowflakes travel exactly the same path, so no two diaries are the same.
Isn't that a beautiful picture? Every snowflake lands on the ground carrying its own journey, its own story.

The physicist Kenneth Libbrecht points out that one snowflake contains more than ten to the eighteenth power water molecules. How much is ten to the eighteenth? A one followed by eighteen zeros. The possible arrangements of a complex branching snowflake are unimaginably many, so the chance of two being exactly alike is practically zero.

But an honest scientist will add a caveat: small, simple columnar crystals that have just formed in a cloud can look very much alike. In 1988, a researcher reported finding two small snow crystals that looked almost identical.

So the more accurate statement is this: complex branching snowflakes are almost never identical, but small, simply shaped crystals can look very much alike. I really like this kind of honesty. When we believers talk about science, we should speak accurately and humbly, without exaggeration. That itself is a witness.
So what does this have to do with us? A great deal!

If God doesn't even repeat a snowflake, would He make people carelessly, like a photocopier? Of course not. You too have your journey, your temperature, your humidity. The mountains and valleys you've walked through have all written lines on the arms of your life. You are one of a kind.
David says this in the Psalms:
I will give thanks to you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made. Your works are wonderful. My soul knows that very well. (Psalm 139:14)

Notice that David doesn't say, "I'm very good-looking," or "I'm very capable." He says, "I am fearfully and wonderfully made." His focus is not on how excellent he is, but on how wonderful God's works are. God knows every snowflake, and He knows your name and your story even better.
3. Beauty no one watches: God doesn't make beauty for applause
The third point, I think, is the most moving part of this unit.

Every year countless snowflakes fall into empty valleys. No photographers, no tourists, no one ever glances at them. Yet they are just as exquisite, with the same six slender arms and the same lovely patterns.

Friends, if you owned a restaurant and there were no customers today, would you still plate every dish beautifully? Probably not. No one's looking anyway. But God isn't like that. Even where no one sees, He still makes beauty as well as it can be made.

In this unit's Verify section there's a very important observation: a snowflake's beauty far exceeds what its existence "requires." To fall, melt, and turn into water, a snowflake really doesn't need to be this pretty.

This kind of beauty, "exquisite even when no one is watching," points to a Creator who delights in making beautiful things. Let's be clear: this is a philosophical inference, not a laboratory "proof" of God. But it's a very natural inference. It's like walking into a house and seeing every corner clean and tidy, even the insides of the drawers neatly arranged; you'd reasonably conclude that whoever lives there is careful and loves beauty.
God makes beauty not for applause, but because He Himself is beautiful and good. Beauty flows naturally out of His character.

This is a great comfort to us. Do you also have many moments that "no one sees"? Quietly caring for aging parents, still praying for your children late at night, doing things at work no one knows about, setting out chairs and washing cups at church without anyone saying thank you.

Brothers and sisters, God watches over the snowflakes even in empty valleys. How could He not see you? Your quiet giving is, in His eyes, like snowflakes falling in a valley: exquisite, precious, and not one will be forgotten.
Now let's bring the snowflake back into daily life. From the 321 vision, I've chosen the three that fit best to share with you.

First, the Bible is my standard. We live in a world that loves to compare: grades, income, houses, children, even the number of likes on social media. Many people's sense of worth is tied up in what others think of them.
But my worth is not decided by what others think; it is decided by God's Word. And what does God's Word say? I am His wonderful work. Whether people "like" me or not, that truth never changes.

Second, humility overcomes pride. Some people think humility means always putting yourself down: "I can't do it, I'm nothing." Actually, that isn't necessarily humility; sometimes it's just another form of being self-centered.

True humility is returning to our proper place: no need to envy someone else's shape, and no need to look down on our own. Let God be God, and let me be me. The star-shaped snowflake needn't envy the column, and the column needn't look down on the plate. Every one was made according to God's own design.

Third, people matter more than tasks. If I am God's unique handiwork, then the person sitting next to me, my spouse, my coworker, that neighbor who often gives me headaches, is also God's unique handiwork.
So let's replace comparison with appreciation. Comparison brings pride or insecurity; appreciation brings gratitude and relationship.
This week, please do one thing: write down three unique things God has placed in you. Then, face to face, affirm something unique about a family member or friend.

I know that for many people the second is harder than the first, especially with your spouse, when the words usually don't come out. That's okay. Start with one sentence: "You know what? There's something about you I really appreciate." Who knows, that night a warm snow might fall in your home.
Brothers and sisters, the next time you see snow, or frost, or ice patterns on a window, or a snowflake photo online, please stop and look closely for thirty seconds.

In those thirty seconds, think of the more than five thousand photos Bentley took in the cold wind; think of Nakaya's words, "Snow crystals are letters sent from heaven"; think of the snowflakes falling in empty valleys, unseen yet still exquisite.
Then ask yourself: Do I often feel ordinary and replaceable? God never makes the same snowflake twice. How does He see me?
The answer is: in His eyes you are one of a kind, His wonderful work. Let's pray together.

Lord who made the snowflakes, thank You for so carefully making me one of a kind. You create exquisite beauty even in valleys no one sees, and You see every quiet sacrifice I make. Take away my heart of comparing myself with others, so that I neither envy nor feel inferior, but live before You as the person You made me to be. Open my eyes, too, to appreciate everyone around me as Your unique handiwork. In Jesus' name, Amen.

1. A snowflake's hexagon comes from the hexagonal lattice of water molecules; beauty is built on order at the tiniest level. What other examples have you seen in life of "order in the small things making the whole beautiful"?
2. The saying "no two snowflakes are alike" needs a qualification to be accurate. Why do you think honesty, accuracy, and not exaggerating are an important witness when Christians talk about science?
3. When did you last feel "ordinary and replaceable"? How does Psalm 139:14 change the way you see yourself? Share something unique about someone around you that you'd like to affirm.
The Peacock's Secret: Blue Without Paint
One thing I have asked of Yahweh, that I will seek after: that I may dwell in Yahweh's house all the days of my life, to see Yahweh's beauty, and to inquire in his temple. (Psalm 27:4)
Brothers and sisters, friends, peace to you! If someone asked you, "Who's the biggest show-off in the animal kingdom?" I'd guess many of you would think first of the peacock.

The moment a peacock spreads his train, every visitor at the zoo stops in their tracks and all the phones go up. Hundreds of "eyespots" shimmer together in blue, green, gold, and bronze. Better still, if you look from a different angle, the colors shift, as if the whole train were alive.
Now let me ask a slightly "cruel" question. Don't worry, it's only imaginary: if we ground a blue peacock feather into powder, what color would the powder be?

Most people would say, "Blue-green powder, of course!" But the answer is startling: you would not get a pile of blue-green dust. What you'd get is mostly dark brown. Those colors aren't in any "paint" at all.
So where is the color? Today we're going to uncover the peacock's secret, and through that secret hear God's reminder for our lives. We'll look at three main points.
Yahweh, how many are your works! In wisdom have you made them all. The earth is full of your riches. (Psalm 104:24)
For our first point, let's take a relaxed little "color class." The colors in the world come, broadly speaking, from two sources.

The first is called "pigment color." In things like carrots and leaves, the molecules absorb certain colors of light and reflect the rest; the color we see is the one reflected back. It's like watercolor or house paint: the color is in the material itself.

The second is called "structural color." This is where it gets wonderful: the material itself may be brown, or even transparent, but it's arranged in regular structures smaller than a wavelength of light, so certain colors reinforce one another and others cancel out. The color isn't "painted on"; it's "arranged into being."
That may sound abstract, so let's understand it with something we all played with as children: soap bubbles.

Does soapy water have any color? No, it's clear. But blow it into a bubble, and you see rainbow colors flowing across it. Why? Because the thickness of that film is close to the wavelength of light, so it reflects all the colors of the rainbow.

A peacock feather holds thousands upon thousands of such precise "films." That's why the color changes when you change your angle. This angle-shifting "iridescence" is the signature of structural color.
This brings something to mind: some beauty isn't painted on from the outside; it grows from within.

Let's keep that in our hearts for now and come back to it properly in the third point. But we can already say this much: Psalm 104 says, "In wisdom have you made them all." The peacock's color isn't a careless swipe of the brush; it's "arranged" with wisdom.
2. Nanoscale craftsmanship: a natural photonic crystal
For our second point, let's put a peacock feather under an electron microscope.

Using electron microscopes, Jian Zi of Fudan University and colleagues found that in the outer layer of the peacock's barbules, tiny rods of melanin are embedded in keratin, arranged in a regular two-dimensional lattice. It's a natural "photonic crystal."

When the spacing of this lattice changes, the color changes with it. For blue, the spacing is about 140 nanometers; for green and yellow, slightly larger; brown comes from fewer layers combined with other effects.

How small is 140 nanometers? Our hair is already very fine, but this spacing is far, far finer than a hair, so fine you need an electron microscope to see it. With arrangements precise to the nanometer, the peacock "paints" the splendor that covers its body.

Speaking of peacocks, there's a fascinating bit of history. In 1860 Darwin wrote to the American botanist Asa Gray that whenever he gazed at a feather in a peacock's tail, it made him feel "sick." Why sick? Because such splendor was hard to explain as "useful for survival."

A big, heavy tail dragging behind you doesn't look very convenient when you're running for your life. Later, in The Descent of Man, Darwin proposed "sexual selection": the peahen's preferences shaped the peacock's train.

Today the mainstream biological explanation is still sexual selection: over time, females preferred more splendid males, so splendid traits were preserved and enhanced. However, studies disagree on exactly what peahens base their choice on, and the details are still being discussed.
Brothers and sisters, here we need a mature attitude. On issues like evolutionary mechanisms, Christians hold different views, and we should be "united on the core, generous on the periphery."

Even if someone accepts the mechanism of sexual selection, they can still ask a question one level up: why do the laws of physics in our universe allow such exquisite structures as photonic crystals to exist? Why can animals and humans perceive beauty at all? Those are questions at the level of philosophy.

So this unit says carefully: "painting" color with nanometer-scale precision is craftsmanship so ingenious that it brings to mind a wise Designer who loves beauty. This is a reasonable inference, a pointer, not a claim that science has "proved" God. But the pointer is very clear.

It's like seeing a picture precisely pieced together from tens of thousands of tiny colored tiles. You don't need to see the painter to think quite naturally, "There must be a very careful artist behind this."
3. Beauty flows from who He is
What David wanted most in life
For our third point, let's return to today's key verse.
One thing I have asked of Yahweh, that I will seek after: that I may dwell in Yahweh's house all the days of my life, to see Yahweh's beauty, and to inquire in his temple. (Psalm 27:4)

David was a king. He had wealth, power, and an army. If you had asked him, "What do you want most in life?" his answer wouldn't have been more wealth or a bigger kingdom, but "to see Yahweh's beauty."

Peacocks are beautiful, but the peacock's beauty is only a shadow; God Himself is Beauty itself. If the shadow is this beautiful, how beautiful must the reality be? No wonder David said this was the one thing he had asked for and would keep seeking.
God looks at the structure within
Remember the thought we tucked away in the first point? A peacock's color isn't in dye on the surface, but in the structure within.
God looks at people the same way. When Samuel went to Jesse's house to anoint a new king, he saw the eldest son, Eliab, tall and handsome, and thought, "Surely this is the one!" But God said to him:
For I don't see as man sees. For man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart. (1 Samuel 16:7)

Our age places enormous weight on "paint": appearance, packaging, image, brand names, filters. A photo can be edited until you don't even recognize yourself. But God doesn't look at the packaging; He looks at the structure within.

And notice one more thing: once a peacock feather is ground up and its structure destroyed, the interference effect disappears, the splendor is gone, and only the dark color of melanin remains. Human life is like that too: however dazzling the outside, if the structure inside collapses, the splendor can't be kept. On the other hand, when the structure inside is right, the splendor comes out naturally.
Next, from the 321 vision, let's choose the three applications that fit best.
Life first, then relationships, then ministry
First, life first, then relationships, then ministry. The peacock's color comes from its inner structure; in the same way, the fruit of ministry comes from inner life.

Sometimes we get very busy at church: busy running events, busy making schedules, busy in meetings. Layer after layer of outer "paint" goes on, while the life inside grows drier and drier. Ministry like that is hard to sustain and hard to make truly shine. The order has to be right: first let God build up my life; then my relationships will be healthy, and then my ministry will bear fruit.
Let Jesus receive all the glory

Second, let Jesus receive all the glory. Have you ever thought about how the peacock's splendor doesn't actually come from the peacock itself? Light shines on it, and it reflects the light back out. Without light, the peacock's train has no color at all in the dark.

We're the same. If there is anything lovely in us, it's because God's light is shining on us. So when people praise us, let's learn to be like the peacock, reflecting the light back and giving the glory to the Lord who is the source of the light.
Changing our mindset: from man's point of view to God's
Third, changing our mindset: from looking at the outside to looking at the heart; from man's point of view to God's point of view.

This isn't only for how we see ourselves; it's also for how we see others. Next time you meet someone, don't rush to score them by their clothes, education, or job title. Ask yourself: how does God see this person? Perhaps the one you look down on has, deep inside, a structure God is carefully building.
This week's action is simple: spend ten quiet minutes each day reading Scripture and praying, focused on "seeing His beauty," and let God build up the life within you.

Ten minutes isn't long; it might be just a bit of your scrolling time. But those ten minutes a day, like the layer upon layer of nano-films in a peacock feather, will slowly and precisely arrange heavenly splendor within you.
Brothers and sisters, this week find a photo of a peacock feather, or better yet a real one, and look at how its colors change from different angles.
Then quiet yourself and ask: How much effort do I spend on the outer "paint"? And how much do I spend letting God build the "structure" within me?
May we all be like David, seeking one thing all our lives: to see His beauty. Let's pray together.

Beautiful Lord, I want to gaze on Your beauty all my life. Thank You for making the peacock's splendor with wisdom, and even more, thank You for looking not at my outward appearance but at my heart. Forgive me for so often caring only about the outer paint while neglecting the life within. Change me and build me from the inside out, so that my life naturally reflects Your splendor, and all the glory goes to You. In Jesus' name, Amen.

2. In your life, what is "outer paint," and what is "inner structure"? How much time and energy do you currently spend on each?
3. What David sought all his life was "to see Yahweh's beauty." If you practice ten quiet minutes a day gazing on God this week, when and how do you plan to start?
The Butterfly's Wings: Stained Glass That Flies
Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new. (2 Corinthians 5:17)

Brothers and sisters, friends, peace to you! Did you ever catch butterflies as a child? I think many of us have had this experience: you finally pinch a butterfly's wings, and when you let go and look, there's a fine layer of powder on your fingertips.
Back then an adult might have said, "Oh no, you've rubbed the powder off, and now it won't fly well!" And we'd watch, a little guilty, as the butterfly wobbled away.
But do you know what that "powder" really is? It isn't dust. It's thousands of tiny scales. What came off on your fingers was actually the little tiles of the butterfly's wing.
The large group of insects that butterflies and moths belong to is called Lepidoptera, a name formed from the Greek words for "scale" and "wing." The meaning is straightforward: scaled wings.
Today we're going to look closely at those wings, and through the story of the caterpillar becoming a butterfly, see God's work of renewal in our lives.
He has made everything beautiful in its time. He has also set eternity in their hearts. (Ecclesiastes 3:11)
For our first point, let's look at how a butterfly's wing is built.

A butterfly's wing is actually a clear membrane. The scales are laid on this membrane row after row, overlapping like roof tiles. Picture the roof of an old house, one tile pressing on the next, neat and orderly. That's what a butterfly's wing looks like, only unimaginably smaller.

Even more interesting: a single scale usually has just one color. So where do the wing's complex patterns come from? The answer is that they're pieced together, like a mosaic, from many single-colored scales.

Have you ever seen a mosaic mural in a church or a park? From a distance it's a complete picture, perhaps a landscape or a person; up close, you discover it's made of little tiles fitted together one by one.
A butterfly's wing is a mosaic mural made of tiny tiles. The difference is that each of the butterfly's "tiles" is so small you need a microscope to see it clearly. And this mural can fly!

So how are these tiny tiles colored? There are two ways. Some scales contain pigment, like a coat of paint; some produce "structural color" through fine microstructures; and some scales use both methods together.

In the last message, on the peacock, we mentioned structural color: color that isn't painted on but "arranged into being" by fine patterns smaller than a wavelength of light. The butterfly's wing uses this craft to the fullest.

Ecclesiastes says, "He has made everything beautiful in its time." The butterfly's beauty is made of thousands upon thousands of tiny details. Each scale looks insignificant on its own, but put in the right place, it becomes part of a picture.
It's the same with us in God's hands. You may feel like one tiny, unremarkable scale, but in God's great picture you have your place, and without you the picture isn't complete.
2. The blue of the Morpho: the secret of the little Christmas trees

For our second point, let's meet a star of the butterfly world: the Morpho of Central and South America. Its wings are a dazzling blue that flashes in the sunlight as the angle changes, like a piece of flying blue sky.

Where does such a bright blue come from? Magnified, the Morpho's scales carry ridge after ridge running lengthwise. On the sides of each ridge are several extremely thin layers, shaped like rows of little Christmas trees.
These layers alternate with air: a layer, then air, then a layer, then air... As light comes in and bounces back and forth between these layers, the blue light reinforces itself until it glows.

A team led by the British physicist Pete Vukusic measured single Morpho scales and found that some structures can reflect as much as about 75% of incoming blue light, across a very wide range of angles.

What does that mean? It means most of the blue light that comes in is precisely sent back out, and from almost any angle you look, you can see that brilliant blue. These structures have even inspired human research into anti-counterfeiting, sensors, and more.
Just think, friends: human engineers designing anti-counterfeiting labels are taking lessons from a butterfly!

A butterfly's wing isn't only beautiful. An insect's wing has to handle flight, warmth, and recognizing its own kind, all while being stunningly beautiful. So many functions, all done just right, on the same pair of thin wings.
As for how these delicate structures are precisely "assembled" during development, that's still a topic scientists are researching today.

Many see this many-sided fittingness as a clue to design. Let's be clear: this is a philosophical inference, not a claim that science has proved something. But it's like looking at a Swiss Army knife, with the blade, the scissors, and the bottle opener all folded in just right; you naturally think there's a careful designer behind it. The butterfly's wing leads us to reasonably infer that wise Creator.
3. From caterpillar to butterfly: a new creation
A total makeover in the chrysalis
The third point is the heart of this whole message.

A butterfly isn't born beautiful. It gains that beauty through a complete transformation. The caterpillar enters the chrysalis, its body is reorganized, and when it comes out, it is something entirely new.

This isn't a caterpillar putting on a butterfly costume, and it isn't a caterpillar working hard to lose weight and grow wings. It's a reorganization from the inside out. What goes in is a worm crawling on the ground; what comes out is a butterfly flying in the sky.
The Bible uses a beautiful phrase to describe those who believe in Christ: a new creation.
Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new. (2 Corinthians 5:17)

Brothers and sisters, believing in Jesus isn't an "upgraded version of the old me." It isn't a caterpillar with two fake wings taped on. It's a new life. The old things have passed away; all things have become new.
So how does this change happen? Do we squeeze it out by gritting our teeth and trying hard? The Bible says:
But we all, with unveiled face seeing the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, even as from the Lord, the Spirit. (2 Corinthians 3:18)

Notice two keys. First, our part is "with unveiled face" to be "seeing the glory of the Lord," that is, looking to the Lord. Second, the source of the change is "from the Lord, the Spirit": it's the Holy Spirit's work within us.
One more key point: "from glory to glory." Change happens step by step, not overnight. Even the caterpillar needs time in the chrysalis.

So if you've been a believer for a while and still feel there's a lot of "caterpillar" in you, don't lose heart. God is still at work. He hasn't given up on you. He intends to take you from glory to glory.
Next, from the 321 vision, let's choose three applications.
The Holy Spirit is my guide

First, the Holy Spirit is my guide. Since transformation comes "from the Lord, the Spirit," the most important thing for me each day isn't to set a hundred rules first, but to ask the Holy Spirit to renew me day by day.
When you get up each morning, you can pray a simple prayer: "Holy Spirit, please guide me today, and keep doing Your transforming work in me."
The eight steps of changing our mindset
Second, the eight steps of changing our mindset: information, revelation, conviction, practice... change takes a process, and it takes repetition.

We often hear a good sermon, feel deeply moved, and think, "Starting today I'm going to be different!" Then two days later we're back to our old ways. That's normal, because change is a process. Hearing is information; God opening our eyes is revelation; agreeing in our hearts is conviction; and then we still have to practice, again and again. Don't give up just because you fall once. A butterfly doesn't break out of its chrysalis in a day either.
Third, selflessness: it is no longer I, but Christ who lives in me. Only when the old self steps aside can the new life spread its wings.

If a caterpillar insisted, "I'm going to stay a caterpillar," it would never fly. It's the same for us. The old self that says, "That's just my personality," or "I just can't change," must learn to step aside and let the life of Christ grow in us.
This week, please pick one old habit you want to change and write down one concrete new practice. Then ask a spiritual companion to pray for you and check in with you every week: "How's it going?"
Change needs companions. The chrysalis stays alone, but we don't. God has placed brothers and sisters around us so we can walk with one another and break out of our cocoons together.
Brothers and sisters, please think back: comparing your life before you believed with your life now, what has God already changed in you?
Maybe your temper, maybe the way you speak, maybe your attitude toward money or toward your family. Every change is a testimony to God's grace.
Then quietly ask yourself: what part of my life is still like a "caterpillar," needing to be handed over to God to be reshaped in the "chrysalis"? Let's pray together.

Lord who makes us new creations, thank You for not giving up on me. You piece together a butterfly's wings from tens of thousands of tiny scales, and You are at work in every detail of my life. I hand my old ways over to You. Holy Spirit, renew me day by day, so that with unveiled face I look to You, and go from glory to glory, becoming more like Jesus. In Jesus' name, Amen.

The Morning Choir: Birdsong and Music
Let everything that has breath praise Yah! Praise Yah! (Psalm 150:6)

Brothers and sisters, friends, peace to you! Have you ever had this experience? It's not yet light, you're still under the covers, and the birds outside the window start to sing. One begins, another joins in, and it gets livelier and livelier, like a morning choir with no conductor.

Some people hear it and think, "How poetic!" Others roll over and pull the pillow over their heads: "Come on, what time is it?" I don't know which kind you are, but today I want to invite you to listen to this morning concert with a different set of ears.
Because behind this concert there are many wonderful scientific discoveries, and, even more, a theme that has never stopped from creation to eternity: praise.
The birds of the sky nest by them. They sing among the branches. (Psalm 104:12)
We'll look at three main points: how birds learn to sing, the musical code hidden in birdsong, and why humans love to sing so much too.

Our first point may surprise many people: many songbirds are not born knowing their songs. They learn them by listening to adult birds when young and practicing over and over, just as children learn to talk.
Many young songbirds have a learning period. During that time they must listen, imitate, and practice before they can sing like adults.

It's like a child learning piano. First they listen to the teacher play, then they try it themselves again and again. At first it's not a tune at all, and everyone at home wants to cover their ears; then it gradually becomes fluent, until at last they can play a whole piece. And birds that never hear a teacher often can't sing a complete song.
And birdsong isn't random chirping. It's built from notes into phrases, and from phrases into complete songs, with a fixed order and rhythm.

Songbirds also have a special voice organ called the "syrinx." The syrinx has two sound sources, left and right, so it can produce two different notes at the same time. Think about it: a human singer can sing only one note at a time, and it takes two people to harmonize, but some birds can sing a "duet" all by themselves!
So why do birds sing? Birdsong has two main functions: claiming territory and attracting a mate. In other words, one song says, "This is my home," and the other says, "Will you marry me?"
Brothers and sisters, young birds learn to sing by listening to a teacher, and we learn to praise by "listening" too.

Where do we learn to praise? From the Psalms in the Bible, from the hymns and songs of the church, and from brothers and sisters around us who keep praising even in suffering. If we rarely "listen," it's hard for our lives to sing a complete song of praise. Someone who often soaks in God's Word will naturally have a song in their mouth.

Here's another interesting point: a young bird learning to sing doesn't sound good at first, but it doesn't give up; it practices again and again. Our praise is like that too. Maybe at first we're just singing along, lips moving while the heart hasn't caught up. That's okay. Keep singing, keep learning, and one day you'll find the song has traveled from your mouth into your heart.

And don't forget: when young birds practice, an adult bird is nearby to model the song. On the road of faith, do you have a "teacher" like that beside you? And are you willing to be an example for others, so that younger brothers and sisters can learn to praise from you?
The hermit thrush and the harmonic series
For our second point, let's meet a very special singer: the hermit thrush of North America.

Researchers analyzing the hermit thrush's song found something remarkable: most of the pitches it chooses fall on the "harmonic series" of a single fundamental. What's the harmonic series? Simply put, it's the same kind of simple whole-number ratios found in human musical scales.
In other words, the "scale" this bird sings is close in principle to human music. This was the first time the phenomenon was demonstrated in an animal with rigorous statistical methods.
But we should also say honestly: scholars still interpret differently whether this means birds have a "musical sense." Scientists are still discussing it, and we're in no hurry to draw conclusions.
Still, this finding at least makes us stop and think: why would a bird in a North American forest use the same simple whole-number ratios as human instruments and human voices?

It's like traveling to a country you've never visited and hearing the locals sing; you don't understand the language, yet the melody feels familiar. This leads us to a reasonable inference: birdsong and human song seem to be built on the same beautiful set of laws, and those laws point to the Creator who established them.
3. Why do humans love to sing?
For our third point, we turn from birds to people.

A Harvard team analyzed a large body of ethnographic data and found that every society they studied had music. What's more, music like lullabies and dance songs shares similar features across different cultures.

Think about it: wherever you go, the songs mothers sing to put their children to sleep are soft, slow, and gentle; the songs people dance to together are lively and rhythmic. Music seems to be a shared human language.
Brain-imaging studies have also found that when music moves us to "goosebumps," the brain's reward system becomes active and releases dopamine.

Have you had that experience? You're singing a certain hymn in a service, and one line suddenly strikes your heart; you get goosebumps all over, and tears fall. That's not because you're too easily moved; it's because God designed that kind of response into our bodies.
Here's something worth pondering: humans everywhere create and enjoy music far beyond what survival requires. You can't eat a symphony, and a lullaby can't shelter you from wind and rain.
This fits very well with the biblical view that people were made for praise. Let's be clear: this is a philosophical inference, not a laboratory proof. But the fit is truly beautiful.
The Bible is full of songs from beginning to end: creation is called to praise, and God's people are called to sing. Most astonishing of all, God Himself rejoices over His people with singing!
Yahweh, your God, is among you, a mighty one who will save. He will rejoice over you with joy. He will calm you in his love. He will rejoice over you with singing. (Zephaniah 3:17)

Brothers and sisters, have you ever thought about this: God rejoices over you with singing? Not because of how well you perform, but because He loves you. We aren't singing solo in a cold, empty universe; we're singing to a God who sings over us.
The birds don't know whom they are praising, but we can know. Praise is giving the voices of creation back to the Lord who made every voice.
speaking to one another in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs; singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord; (Ephesians 5:19)
I will sing to Yahweh as long as I live. I will sing praise to my God while I have any being. (Psalm 104:33)
Next, from the 321 vision, let's choose the three applications that fit best.
Let Jesus receive all the glory
First, let Jesus receive all the glory. The focus of praise is God, not whether my singing sounds good.

Some brothers say, "Pastor, I'm tone-deaf. My singing scares the people next to me." That's okay! What God wants is "making melody in your heart": He wants the heart, not perfect pitch. On the other hand, those who sing beautifully need to be careful not to let praise become a performance, where people see me instead of Jesus.
Second, give thanks in everything. Turn gratitude into a daily song, and give the glory to Jesus.

Here, let's each honestly ask ourselves: is my mouth used mostly for complaining and criticizing, or for thanksgiving and praise? If everything we said in a day were recorded, which would there be more of, complaints or thanks? The birds sing every morning. Could we have a song of thanks every day too?

Third, 235 spiritual companions (walking the road of faith together, not alone). Ephesians says we should be "speaking to one another"; praise isn't only a solo affair, it's something we sing together.

The morning birds sing one after another, answering each other; we too need to praise in one voice with our brothers and sisters. When you're low and can't sing, a spiritual companion can sing for you; when they're weak, you can sing for them.
This week, please begin each morning with a hymn or a psalm, and invite a family member or friend to sing with you.

Tomorrow morning, open a window or step outside and listen quietly to the birds for one minute. Then sing a hymn or worship song you love. Let the birds' choir gain one more singer who knows whom they are praising.
Brothers and sisters, the last verse of the Psalms says, "Let everything that has breath praise Yah!"

The birds sing with their breath, though they don't know whom they're praising. But we are people who have breath and also know God. We know who gives us breath, and who rejoices over us with singing.
From today on, may we sing in good times and in hard times; sing at church, and in the kitchen, in the car, at the office, and in our hearts. Let's pray together.

Lord who gives me breath, You rejoice over me with singing, and I will sing to You. Thank You for making the birdsong of the morning and for placing music in our hearts. Forgive me for so often using my mouth to complain and criticize, and so rarely to give thanks and praise. Help me praise You with my lips and my heart in harmony, give me a new song in good times and hard times alike, and let me sing Your praise with my brothers and sisters with one heart and one mind. In Jesus' name, Amen.
1. Many songbirds learn to sing by hearing adult models and practicing repeatedly. Where, and from whom, did you "learn" to praise?
2. If everything you said in a day were recorded, how much would be complaining and criticizing, and how much thanksgiving and praise? How would you like to change that ratio?
3. Zephaniah 3:17 says God rejoices over His people with singing. How do you feel when you think of God rejoicing over you? Whom would you like to invite to sing a hymn with you this week?
A World of Color: Beauty Seen and Unseen
For with you is the spring of life. In your light we will see light. (Psalm 36:9)
Brothers and sisters, friends, peace to you! Let's begin with a little exercise of the imagination. Please close your eyes for a moment.

Imagine you wake up tomorrow morning and find the whole world has turned black, white, and gray. The sky is gray, the leaves are gray, the sunset is gray. Your favorite mango: gray. Your child's smiling face: gray too. All right, please open your eyes.
Don't you feel relieved? The colors are all still here! We see color every time we open our eyes, and we rarely stop to think what a great gift that is.

Even more amazing: the same yellow flower is plain yellow to your eyes, but to a bee, there may be a "bull's-eye" in the middle that you can't see. It turns out that in the same world, different eyes see different things.
Jesus once told His disciples to go and look at the flowers of the field:

Why are you anxious about clothing? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow. They don't toil, neither do they spin, yet I tell you that even Solomon in all his glory was not dressed like one of these. (Matthew 6:28–29)
King Solomon's royal robes couldn't match a wildflower. Today let's "consider" these flowers together, consider these colors, and consider the God who gives us color. We'll look at three main points.
1. Three paintbrushes paint the whole colorful world
First point: how exactly do we see color?

On the retina of our eyes are three kinds of "cone cells" responsible for color vision. They are most sensitive to short, medium, and long wavelengths of light, with absorption peaks at about 420, 534, and 564 nanometers.
Then the brain compares the strength of the signals from these three kinds of cells and, like mixing paint, produces an endless variety of colors.

We can understand this principle with an analogy: the three kinds of cone cells are like three paintbrushes with only red, green, and blue paint. But the brain is a brilliant painter. By mixing them in different proportions, it paints the whole world in color.

Just think, friends: with only three brushes, it paints the blue of the sky, the green of the leaves, the orange of the sunset, the pink of a baby's cheeks, and hundreds of colors we don't even have names for. What an ingenious design.
There's another very important thing we often overlook: color needs light. Without light there is no color. When we see the color of an object, we are actually seeing the light it reflects back.

Turn off the lights at night: is that beautiful red shirt in your closet still red? In the dark it has no color at all. Objects can't produce color on their own; it shows only when light shines on them.
That's exactly what today's key verse means:
For with you is the spring of life. In your light we will see light. (Psalm 36:9)

We see color because there is light; we know God because He first shines on us. When someone can see God's beauty and understand God's love, it isn't because they're especially clever, but because God's light first shone into their heart.
For our second point, let's switch eyes and look at the world through the eyes of a bee.

Bees and other hymenopteran insects mostly have three kinds of photoreceptors too, but their bands differ from ours: their absorption peaks are roughly in the ultraviolet (about 340 nanometers), blue, and green. And most of them have no red receptor.

So bees can see ultraviolet light, which we can't; yet bees have trouble telling red apart, which we can spot at a glance. Bees and humans each have their own three paintbrushes, and so they paint different worlds.
A landing runway on the flower

This leads to a fascinating discovery. Many petals absorb ultraviolet at the center and reflect it around the edges. To human eyes the flower may be just plain yellow, but to an insect it forms a "bull's-eye" pattern, like the runway lights at an airport guiding a plane in to land.

A bee flies over, takes one look, and says, "Oh, right here! Land in the middle!" Field experiments also show that changing this ultraviolet pattern affects how often pollinators visit. Of course, how strongly the pattern matters varies from plant to plant, and scientists are still studying it.
Clues in how things fit together
Think about it, friends: the colors of flowers, the eyes of pollinators, and the nature of light fit together like a key in a lock.

Many see this mutual correspondence as a clue to intelligent design. It's a philosophical inference, not a scientific "proof." But it's like receiving a gift whose wrapping has a pattern you can see only with a special pair of glasses made just for you; you'd surely think, "The giver really took trouble for me!"
3. Different beauty prepared for different eyes
His beauty is more than we can see
For our third point, let's consider what all this is saying.
God painted patterns on flowers for bees that humans cannot see, and He prepared countless colors for humans. God's beauty is more than we can see.

This is a very important reminder. So often we assume that "I don't see it" means "it doesn't exist." But the bull's-eye on that flower is still there even though you can't see it; the bee sees it perfectly clearly.
God saw everything that he had made, and, behold, it was very good. (Genesis 1:31)
God saw everything He had made, and it was very good. He sees the whole picture: the beauty humans can see, the beauty bees can see, and beauty none of us can see, which only He Himself enjoys.
Unseen doesn't mean God isn't working

Brothers and sisters, this is a great help for our life of faith. Sometimes we pray about something for a long time and nothing seems to happen; sometimes we're in a hard place and can't see a way out, or see what God is doing.

But not seeing doesn't mean God isn't at work. Like the ultraviolet pattern on a flower, God may be painting a pattern in your life that you can't see yet. One day, when He opens your eyes, you'll discover, "He was here all along!"

I love to think of it this way: the flower that is just plain yellow to human eyes is a clear invitation to a bee: "Come here!" The same thing, seen through different eyes, looks completely different. Our situations are like that too. Seen with human eyes, it may look like nothing but chaos; ask God for new eyes, and perhaps you'll see the path He has already painted.

Let's go back to the lilies Jesus spoke about. When Jesus told His disciples to look at the flowers, He wasn't giving them a botany lesson; He was telling them not to worry. If God dresses a flower that neither toils nor spins more beautifully than Solomon, how much more will He care for us?
A God who takes so much care over flowers and bees, would He not care for you? Your food and clothing, your tomorrow, your family: He sees them all.
Next, from the 321 vision, let's choose the three applications that fit best.
From man's point of view to God's point of view
First, change from man's point of view to God's point of view. I see only part; God sees the whole picture.

Human eyes have only three paintbrushes; we can't see ultraviolet, and we can't see much of what God is doing. So when we make judgments, we should be a little more humble: what I see isn't necessarily everything. When something doesn't make sense, don't rush to a conclusion; ask instead, "Lord, how do You see this?"

Second, relationships matter more than things. Flowers and bees need each other: the flower gives the bee nectar, and the bee pollinates the flower. The flower even paints a landing runway for the bee. What a considerate relationship!

We too help one another become whole in our relationships. With family, coworkers, brothers and sisters, have we "painted a runway" for the people around us, making it easier for them to come near and find help? Or do we care only about our own things and neglect the people beside us?
Third, give thanks in everything. Turn the colors we take for granted into daily reasons to give thanks.

We often give thanks for big things: a promotion, getting into a school, being healed from illness. Of course we should give thanks for those. But can we also give thanks for the blue of the sky, the green of the leaves, the colors of a bowl of rice? A person who gives thanks for colors will find their life growing more and more colorful.
This week, each day, please take a photo of a color that moves you, add one line of thanks, and share it with a friend.

You can photograph the sky, flowers, a plate of food, even your child's colorful scribbles. By the end of the week you'll have seven photos of thanks, and your friend will have received seven small blessings.

Brothers and sisters, when you get home today, or tomorrow morning, go to a window or step outside and count how many different shades of green you can see. You'll be surprised how many colors are hiding under the single word "green."
Then quietly ask yourself: Do I assume something doesn't exist just because I "can't see" it? Could God be doing work in my life that I haven't seen yet?
May God open our eyes to see not only the beauty of creation, but His works and His heart. Let's pray together.

Source of light, thank You for letting me see this colorful world. Thank You for giving me three paintbrushes, and for painting runways on flowers for the bees; Your beauty is more than I can see. Forgive me for so often taking Your grace for granted, and forgive me for doubting Your presence because I cannot see it. Open my eyes to see not only the beauty of creation, but Your works and Your heart. In Jesus' name, Amen.
1. The human eye sees color through three kinds of cone cells, and without light there is no color. What new insight does this give you into "in your light we will see light"?
2. Bees can see the ultraviolet bull's-eye on flowers, but humans can't. Has there been a time in your life when you "couldn't see" God at work, and only understood later?
3. What "colors you take for granted" do you plan to give thanks for this week? Which friend would you like to share your thanksgiving photos with?
The Colors of the Sky: Blue Skies, Sunsets, and the Rainbow After Rain
I set my rainbow in the cloud, and it will be a sign of a covenant between me and the earth. (Genesis 9:13)
Brothers and sisters, friends, peace to you! Let me ask you: what is the biggest, longest-running, and completely free show in the world?

The answer is right above our heads: the sky. By day the sky is blue; in the evening, as the sun goes down, the horizon turns orange-red and gold; when the rain clears, a rainbow arches across the sky. These colors are on show every day, and no one has ever charged admission.

But has a child ever asked you, "Dad, why is the sky blue?" or "Mom, why does it turn red when the sun goes down?" Plenty of grown-ups get stumped and can only say, "Because... because God likes blue!"
That answer isn't actually wrong! But today we're going to understand a bit more. Since sunlight itself is nearly white, where do the blue sky and the red sunset really come from?
The heavens declare the glory of God. The expanse shows his handiwork. (Psalm 19:1)
The psalmist says the sky "declares" and "shows." Today let's listen to what the sky is saying. We'll look at three main points.
For our first point, let's start with sunlight. Sunlight looks white, but white light is actually a mixture of all the colors.

The molecules in the air "scatter" light, that is, toss it in every direction. And the shorter the wavelength, the more strongly the light is scattered. The strength of the scattering is inversely proportional to the fourth power of the wavelength.

Blue light has a wavelength of about 450 nanometers, and red light about 700. Do the math, and blue light is scattered about 6 times more strongly than red. So when you look up, the whole sky is full of blue light being tossed back and forth.
A sieve that catches blue balls
That sounds a bit like a physics class, so let's try an analogy. The atmosphere is like a sieve that specializes in "catching blue balls."

Sunlight contains balls of every color, all rolling through the sieve together. The blue balls are the easiest to catch and toss in every direction. So whichever way you look up, there are blue balls everywhere, and the sky is blue.

And in the evening? When the sun is low, its light has to slant through much more air; the path is longer. In our analogy, the sieve gets longer, and all the blue balls are caught along the way, so the only balls that finally roll up to our eyes are red and orange ones. That's why at sunset the horizon glows orange-red.
This scattering law was proposed by the British physicist Lord Rayleigh in 1871.
At this point, friends who like to think might ask, "Pastor, by that logic, violet light has an even shorter wavelength and is scattered even more, so shouldn't the sky be violet?"

Great question! There are several reasons: sunlight contains less violet to begin with; some violet light is absorbed high in the atmosphere; and most important, the combined response of the three kinds of cone cells in our eyes to the sky's spectrum makes us see a whitish blue.
Friends, this is truly wonderful. The blue of the sky is produced by sunlight, the atmosphere, and our eyes all "working together."

This unit makes a deep observation: the same physical laws, on the one hand, let sunlight pass through the atmosphere to nourish life on earth, and on the other, make the sky display beauty every day. Usefulness and loveliness appear together.

This is seen as a clue to a good Creator. Of course, it's a philosophical inference. But when a good chef makes a dish that is both nourishing and delicious, you don't say, "That's just a coincidence." You say, "This chef really cares."
2. The rainbow: the one that belongs to you
For our second point, let's look at the rainbow.

A rainbow forms when sunlight enters a raindrop, is first refracted, reflects inside the drop, and is refracted again on the way out. Because different colors of light bend by different angles, they separate and line up into the colors we see.
Every little raindrop is like a tiny prism. Countless raindrops in the sky, together splitting the sunlight, paint an arc across the heavens.

Here's an even more romantic fact: the primary bow appears with the sun at your back, on a circular arc about 42 degrees from the "antisolar point." What does that mean? It means the rainbow's position is determined by where your eyes are and where the sun is.

So the rainbow each person sees is really one that belongs to their own position. You and the person standing next to you are seeing light sent by different raindrops. You think you're looking at the same rainbow, but actually God has given each of you your own.
Think about it: isn't that beautiful? God's promise isn't a group photo; it's a handwritten letter to each person.
3. The rainbow is a sign of a covenant kept
Our third point is the meaning of the rainbow in the Bible.

After the flood, God made a covenant with Noah and every living creature, promising never again to destroy the whole earth with a flood, and He set the rainbow in the clouds as the sign of this covenant.
I set my rainbow in the cloud, and it will be a sign of a covenant between me and the earth. (Genesis 9:13)
Please notice one detail: rainbows always appear after rain. No rain, no rainbow.

God never promised that it would never rain in our lives, but He did promise to remember His covenant in the rain. That's a very real comfort. Some people think that once you believe in Jesus you'll never face storms, and then they stumble at the first difficulty. But the Bible never said that. God's promise is: the rain will come, but My covenant will not change.

Remember how a rainbow forms? It needs sunlight, and it needs raindrops; you can't do without either. Sun without rain, and you see no rainbow; rain without sun, and you see no rainbow either. The rainbows in our lives are like that too: in the rain, God's light shines in and refracts into that band of hope.

And notice, friends: to see the primary bow, you have to have your back to the sun. Sometimes in our troubles we feel as if God isn't in front of us, as if we've turned our backs to the light. But it's exactly then, if you lift your head and look toward the rain, that you'll find God's promise hanging right there.
So, brothers and sisters, when it rains, don't just look down at the puddles on the ground; remember to look up. The covenant-keeping God has never forgotten a word He has spoken.
Even more wonderful, the rainbow doesn't appear in the Bible only in Noah's day. When the prophet Ezekiel saw a vision of God's glory, he said:
As the appearance of the rainbow that is in the cloud in the day of rain, so was the appearance of the brightness all around. This was the appearance of the likeness of Yahweh's glory. (Ezekiel 1:28)
When John saw the throne in heaven in Revelation, he also said:
There was a rainbow around the throne, like an emerald to look at. (Revelation 4:3)

From Genesis to Revelation, the rainbow is always there. On earth it is the sign of the covenant; in heaven it encircles God's throne. This tells us that the God who remembers His covenant in the rain is the very God who reigns on the throne.
Next, from the 321 vision, let's choose the three applications that fit best.
First, the Bible is my standard. God's promises are written in the Bible, more reliable than the weather.

The forecast says tomorrow will be sunny, and then it pours; we've all had that happen. Human predictions miss, but God's Word does not. When your circumstances tell you "there's no hope" and the Bible says "God is faithful," which will we choose to believe? Let God's Word be the standard by which we judge everything.
From the temporary to the eternal
Second, change from the temporary to the eternal. The rain is temporary; God's covenant is forever.

The rain you're going through now might be worry over illness, pressure at work, conflict at home, or financial hardship. That rain is real, but it's temporary. God's covenant is eternal. When we turn our eyes from the temporary to the eternal, the rain isn't so frightening anymore.
Third, multiplication. Tell someone going through a hard time about God's faithfulness in the storm.

Have you experienced God's faithfulness in the rain? That experience isn't only for you; God wants you to pass it on. Just as the rainbow is for everyone to see, your testimony can become a rainbow in someone else's rain.
This week, please write down a time you experienced God's faithfulness in difficulty. Then share it with a friend who needs encouragement.
It doesn't need to be long or eloquent. One true story has more power than a hundred "hang in there"s.
Brothers and sisters, find a moment today to look at the sky. If it's evening, quietly watch a whole sunset.

As you look at the blue sky, remember the God who lets sunlight nourish life and also makes the sky beautiful; as you look at the sunset, remember the God who still paints beauty at the end of every day; when you see a rainbow, remember the God who remembers His covenant in the rain.
Then quietly ask yourself: What "rain" is falling in my life right now? Can I see God's covenant rainbow in the rain? Let's pray together.

Covenant-keeping God, Your promises never change. Thank You for putting on the show of blue skies and sunsets for us every day, and thank You for setting the rainbow in the clouds to remind us of Your faithfulness. When I go through storms, help me look up and see the signs of Your faithfulness, and keep trusting You in hardship. And use my experiences to become a rainbow in someone else's rain. In Jesus' name, Amen.
1. The same physical laws let sunlight nourish life and make the sky beautiful every day. What other examples have you seen in life of "useful and lovely" appearing together?

2. God didn't promise there would be no more rain, but He did promise to remember His covenant in the rain. What is the "rain" in your life right now? Which of God's promises can you hold on to in the rain?
3. Please share a time you experienced God's faithfulness in difficulty. Which friend who needs encouragement would you like to tell about it this week?
Taste and See: The Goodness of Flavor
Oh taste and see that Yahweh is good. Blessed is the man who takes refuge in him. (Psalm 34:8)

Brothers and sisters, friends, peace to you! Today's message comes with a small risk: halfway through, you may start getting hungry. If anyone is secretly thinking about what to have for lunch, I completely understand.
Picture this: you pick up a perfectly ripe mango and take a bite. Sweet juice floods your mouth, the aroma rushes into your nose, and you can't help closing your eyes: "Mmm, delicious!"
In that brief moment, an entire, finely tuned sensory system is working all at once.

Let's think about something else. Eating really only needs to supply energy. If God just wanted us to stay alive, He could have made all food as tasteless as plain water, as long as it was nutritious enough. But God didn't do that. He gave food thousands of flavors and aromas.
Out of the ground Yahweh God made every tree to grow that is pleasant to the sight, and good for food. (Genesis 2:9)
Notice that the fruit isn't only "good for food"; it's also "pleasant to the sight." God cares not only about our stomachs but about our joy. Today, in three main points, let's taste God's goodness.
For our first point, let's get to know the tongue. Humans have five basic tastes: sweet, sour, salty, bitter, and umami.

The taste cells on the tongue each have specialized receptors that tell different tastes apart. For example, the sweet receptor is made of two proteins joined together. It's like a lock that needs two parts fitted together before it can open the door marked "sweet."
Of the five tastes, the one people like least is probably bitter. We've all seen the scrunched-up face of a child taking medicine.

But bitterness is actually a form of protection. Humans have more than twenty kinds of bitter receptors, and many toxic substances are bitter. Bitterness is like an alarm reminding us, "Careful! This might not be safe to eat!"

This makes me think that God gives us not only sweetness but also bitterness, and the bitter things are often there to protect us. Life is like that too: some "bitter" experiences, looked back on later, turn out to have been God's protection.

Let's try a little interactive exercise. Imagine right now that you're holding a freshly cut lemon. You bring it to your mouth and take a big bite. Is anyone's mouth already starting to pucker? We haven't eaten anything, just thought about it, and our bodies are already responding.

A single thought can set the whole system in motion. That shows how finely tuned God has made us. He didn't just throw a tongue together for us; He assigned a dedicated "receiver" to each kind of taste, so that we can tell them apart, enjoy them, and be warned before danger arrives.

Think about it, friends: when God designed the tongue, He gave it sweetness for enjoyment and bitterness for protection. That isn't an indifferent engineer; it's a loving and thoughtful heavenly Father. Like a good mother who cooks tasty meals for her children and also warns them, "Don't touch that!"
2. The nose is the real star
Flavor is mostly in the nose
For our second point, let me tell you a fact that may turn your thinking upside down: much of what we think of as "taste" actually depends on the nose.

Food aromas travel from the back of the mouth into the nasal cavity. That's why, when a cold blocks your nose, food tastes bland. Your tongue isn't broken; the star of the show, your nose, has simply taken the day off.
Five keys and a pipe organ

Here's an analogy: taste is like five basic piano keys, but smell is like an entire pipe organ. With only five keys, you can play only so many tunes; but add a whole pipe organ, and when the two play together, they perform a dish's rich "symphony of flavor."
Next time you enjoy a good dish, why not give your nose a round of applause in your heart!
In 1991 the American scientists Linda Buck and Richard Axel discovered a large family of olfactory receptor genes, for which they received the 2004 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

Humans have about four hundred working olfactory receptor genes. How do we recognize so many different smells? Through "combinations" of different receptors. Just as an alphabet of a couple dozen letters can spell tens of thousands of words, a few hundred odor receptors in combination can recognize all kinds of smells.
You may have seen a claim in the news: "Humans can distinguish more than a trillion odors." That was the estimate of a 2014 study, and it was widely reported at the time.

But later, other scholars pointed out problems with the study's calculation, and what the real number is remains unclear. When we talk about science we have to be honest; we can't trumpet a number just because it's impressive.
Still, one thing is certain: the human nose is far more sensitive than was once thought.

There's a spiritual reminder here too. When we witness to others about God, we don't need to exaggerate. God's works are wonderful enough on their own; if we simply tell them honestly, that's enough to fill people with wonder. Truth itself is a kind of beauty.

This unit makes an observation well worth pondering: if eating were only for survival, food wouldn't really need to be so delicious. Rich flavors and enjoyment point to a generous Creator who delights in our joy.

Let's be clear: this is a philosophical inference, not a laboratory proof. But the inference is very close to our experience. When a friend invites you to a meal and doesn't just fill you up, but specially prepares the dishes you love, you know, "He really cares about me."

Think about it: why does the soup Mom makes always seem better than anything you can buy? The ingredients may be about the same, but you know her care is in that bowl: she remembers you don't eat cilantro, she remembers you like extra green onion. A flavor can hold a heart's intention. The thousands of flavors in creation hold the Creator's heart as well.
3. God is glad for us to enjoy
For our third point, let's move from flavors to tasting God's heart.

Some people picture God as a stern, stingy master, as if He won't let anyone touch anything good, and as if enjoying anything should make you feel guilty. But the Bible tells us God is not that kind of God.
...but on the living God, who richly provides us with everything to enjoy. (1 Timothy 6:17)
"Richly provides us with everything to enjoy": those are the Bible's own words. God created fruit "pleasant to the sight" and "good for food." He is glad for us to enjoy everything He gives.
Taste and see the Lord's goodness
But the Bible wants to take us one level deeper. Just as the body's tongue can taste sweetness, the spiritual life can also "taste" God's goodness, that is, come to know Him through experience.
Oh taste and see that Yahweh is good. Blessed is the man who takes refuge in him. (Psalm 34:8)

Friends, someone could spend half an hour describing how delicious a mango is, and it still wouldn't compare with taking one bite yourself. Faith is the same: hearing that God is good and personally tasting that God is good are two completely different things.
How sweet are your promises to my taste, more than honey to my mouth! (Psalm 119:103)
God's Word can be "tasted" too. When you're in a hard place and read a verse that suddenly comforts and lights up your heart, that's tasting the sweetness of God's Word.

Remember the blocked nose we talked about? When a cold blocks your nose, even the best dish has no flavor. The spiritual life can get "blocked" too: busyness, worry, and sin can leave us reading the Bible without tasting anything, and gathering for worship without being moved. The problem often isn't that God's Word has gone bland; it's that our spiritual senses are blocked.

What do we do then? Just as a cold calls for rest and water, we need to become quiet, confess to God, pour out our hearts to Him, and let the Holy Spirit clear our senses once again. When your "nose" clears, you'll be amazed to discover that God's Word was this sweet all along.
Next, from the 321 vision, let's choose the three applications that fit best.
First, the order of relationships: first enjoy God, then enjoy what God gives. Don't let the gift replace the Giver.

This is a subtle reminder. God is glad for us to enjoy His gifts, but if we love the gift more than the One who gave it, the order is out of place. It's like a child who gets a bicycle from his father and then rides it every day but never talks to his father again; that father would surely be heartbroken.

Let's each quietly ask ourselves: when was the last time I thanked God simply for who He is, and not for what He's given me? If you think hard and can't remember, perhaps that's God gently reminding us: come back to the Lord who gives the grace.
Second, give thanks in everything. Grace before meals is not a formality; it acknowledges that everything comes from Him.
In everything give thanks, for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus toward you. (1 Thessalonians 5:18)

Sometimes we pray before meals so fast that even we don't know what we said, because the food is getting cold. This week, let's try slowing down and sincerely giving thanks for each dish and for each person who prepared the food.
Third, people matter more than tasks. Good food is best shared, and one meal can build a relationship.
When Jesus was on earth, He often ate with people. A dinner table can often open people's hearts better than a conference room.

Many people first step into a church not because they heard a brilliant sermon, but because someone invited them to a hot meal. At the dinner table there is no pulpit and no distance; a simple "Here, have some more" often opens a heart that was closed.
This week, please invite a friend or neighbor for a meal. Give thanks together before eating, and afterward share one experience of "tasting the Lord's goodness."

It doesn't have to be a feast; a bowl of noodles or a plate of dumplings will do. What matters isn't how lavish the food is, but that you give the other person a chance to taste the Lord's goodness too.
Brothers and sisters, at your next meal, when you take the first bite, please close your eyes, savor it slowly, and name three flavors you taste.
In that moment, think of the five keys on your tongue and the pipe organ in your nose, and think of the God who richly provides us with everything to enjoy.
Then ask yourself: Have I only "heard" that God is good, or have I personally "tasted" His goodness? Let's pray together.

God who richly provides everything, thank You for giving me the ability to taste, to smell, and to enjoy. Thank You for not only filling us up, but giving us thousands of flavors and aromas. Forgive me for so often taking Your gifts for granted, and forgive me for sometimes loving the gifts more than You. Help me enjoy not only Your gifts but You, the Giver; let me taste the sweetness of Your Word every day, and share this goodness with the people around me. In Jesus' name, Amen.
